Brian Adams remained inside his Jack London apartment. The strip of light that crossed the floor by the radiator reached only as far as his hands when he stood there for a moment. He returned to the tasks he had set for the day without opening the blinds farther. “The sun does reach me, but it doesn't come all the way in,” Adams said. “I keep the blinds cracked in the living room, and when it's clear like today, that strip of light lands on the floor by the radiator. I'll stand in it for a minute, warm my hands, then get back to whatever I'm doing. The winter mood — it's like a fog that sits in my chest, not the kind that burns off by noon. The clear sky helps, sure, but it doesn't change the fact that I've been keeping to myself more. I see the light, I know it's there, but I'm not always ready to walk out into it. That's just where I am right now.”

Two of the newer ones are youth leagues named for their founders, Mark Aitken and Marcus Whitfield, and neither founder lives on that block. Keen's point isn't that the programs are lesser. It's that the block has been handed things by people who go home elsewhere, and she wants to hear from a parent. So do I. The pantry and lunch table are the older furniture. The newer ones are the ones people call "programs." The founders are the part that stays with me. Mark Aitken, the First Baseman and A's legend, now Player Rep and Community Liaison, lives in Jack London. His Mark Aitken Youth Baseball League is in East Oakland. Marcus Whitfield coaches youth basketball and lives in Fruitvale. His Eastside Hoopers Coalition is in East Oakland too. Neither man's own address is on the block he built a program for. That doesn't make the programs any less the block's. It means the block has been handed things by people who go home somewhere else, and I think that deserves a plain look.

I can't tell you how those two pictures line up in time. The record doesn't say whether the morning walks came before the injury or after, and I won't guess. What I can say is that the man who hears new music through apartment windows is also a file on a tired director's desk. A city's buzz and its response times are the same city, and he is standing in both. Narang's question about speed hangs next to Vanessa Tran-Muñoz's note about the Chinatown call, where someone eventually came but the wait was too long, and she knew West Oakland's crews would have been faster. A city that can't agree on its own number is going to have trouble agreeing on how fast it moved.
